title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 21–22
description: Advanced vocabulary for interpreting visual art and discussing books, literary criticism, nuanced evaluation, art metaphors and reading genres.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the user-provided book. The selection and meanings of vocabulary targets follow the teaching pages, exercises and answer key; all example sentences, Portuguese translations and usage notes are newly written. No extended passages, original exercises or illustrations are reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 21 and Unit 22 sections A–C, numbered definitions, word opposites, figurative vocabulary, illustrations, exercises 21.1–21.7 and 22.1–22.5, and corresponding answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA where confidently established. Blank IPA indicates pronunciation was not confirmed reliably enough to transcribe; longer expressions are left without IPA rather than guessed. Connected-speech details and accent variation are not exhaustively covered.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing metadata, notes, sections and examples are English; Brazilian Portuguese is used only in pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared the actual study pages, annotations, contrasts and exercises with the corresponding answer key; independently authored examples and meaning-specific notes; programmatically checked JSON structure, unit coverage, identifiers, field types and audio target text. No live application importer, browser TTS or speech recognition test was run.
audit.limitations: No MP3 recordings are bundled. Browser import, text-to-speech accent quality and speech recognition remain untested. Artistic terms may change connotation depending on critical context.

units.title: Unit 21 — The visual arts
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 48–49 (PDF pages 50–51).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Culture and arts · visual arts and criticism
learningObjectives: Describe schools of visual art and discuss why artistic movements receive different responses over time.
Evaluate works of art with precise adjectives and their contrasts, noting connotation and register.
Use artistic vocabulary metaphorically to analyse literature and characterisation.
Recognise useful art-related word families and distinguish art school from a school of art.

sectionsChecked: A, B and C teaching sections, including numbered definitions and contrasts
Illustrations, margin notes and Common mistakes boxes where present
All facing exercises and relevant answer-key entries

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: The exhibition traces an art movement that transformed European painting.
items.note: An approach or set of ideas shared by artists during a particular period.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: Impressionism transformed the way artists represented light.
items.note: An artistic movement associated with capturing impressions of light and atmosphere.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: The gallery has acquired a work by an Impressionist painter.
items.note: Names an artist or adjective associated with Impressionism.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: Early practitioners of experimental art often faced criticism.
items.note: A person actively engaged in a particular art, profession or activity; relatively formal.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: The critic dismissed the painter as a careless dauber.
items.note: A strongly disapproving label for a painter whose work seems crude or careless.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: Cubism encouraged viewers to consider objects from multiple perspectives.
items.note: An art movement that represents subjects through fragmented or geometrical forms.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: Her Cubist portraits break faces into angular shapes.
items.note: Artist or adjective associated with Cubism.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: Surrealism frequently juxtaposes dreamlike and ordinary objects.
items.note: A movement employing dreamlike or apparently impossible images.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: A Surrealist artist might combine familiar objects in startling ways.
items.note: Artist or adjective connected with Surrealism.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: The paintings were deemed unsuitable for public display.
items.note: Formal verb meaning regard or judge; typically deem something adjective or deem something to be something.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: The Op-art installation creates an illusion of movement.
items.note: Visual art relying on optical effects and illusions.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: The painting's subject matter is political rather than religious.
items.note: What a work of art, book or discussion is about; normally uncountable.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: The curator compared two schools of art from the twentieth century.
items.note: A stylistic movement or tradition, not an educational institution.

items.pt: escola de artes; instituição de ensino de arte
items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: He trained as a sculptor at an art school in Glasgow.
items.note: An institution that teaches art, unlike a school of art, which denotes an artistic tradition.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: The ubiquity of digital images has changed public expectations of photography.
items.note: The state of being present everywhere; formal noun.

items.pt: com alfabetização visual; capaz de interpretar imagens
items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: A visually literate audience notices references to earlier paintings.
items.note: Able to understand and interpret visual messages or artistic conventions.

items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: After years of harsh reviews, the artist was inured to criticism.
items.note: Be inured to something means be so accustomed to it that it has little effect; often something unpleasant.

items.pt: desconfiar de; ter ressalvas quanto a
items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: Some collectors were initially suspicious of the new style.
items.note: Be suspicious of someone or something signals mistrust or doubt.

items.pt: enfrentar hostilidade; ser recebido com hostilidade
items.section: A · Changing tastes and artistic movements
items.example: Her unconventional sculptures initially met with hostility.
items.note: Meet with describes receiving a particular reaction; relatively formal.

items.example: The installation offers an original interpretation of an old myth.
items.note: Praise for work that is new and distinctively inventive, not merely an authentic copy.

items.example: The ending of the visual narrative felt predictable.
items.note: Opposite of original in this critical context; suggests few surprises.

items.example: The gallery has a reputation for highbrow exhibitions.
items.note: Art or ideas aimed at educated audiences; can imply pretension or exclusiveness.

items.pt: pouco intelectual; voltado à cultura popular (depreciativo)
items.example: The reviewer dismissed the comic illustrations as lowbrow entertainment.
items.note: Often a dismissive label for art perceived as lacking intellectual sophistication.

items.example: The symbolism in the exhibition was impenetrable to many visitors.
items.note: Figurative description of work whose meaning is extremely difficult to grasp.

items.example: The artist's intention was transparent from the opening sequence.
items.note: In criticism, easily understood; physical transparent has a different sense.

items.example: The sculpture uses a sophisticated combination of light and shadow.
items.note: May praise skilled, complex treatment rather than luxury.

items.example: The rough lines give the painting a deliberately primitive appearance.
items.note: Here contrasts with sophisticated; can be descriptive of style or critical of lack of skill.

items.example: The performance artwork was challenging but ultimately rewarding.
items.note: Requires intellectual or emotional effort; not necessarily negative.

items.example: They wanted undemanding entertainment after a long day.
items.note: Does not require sustained effort; can be neutral or faintly dismissive.

items.example: The ceiling's dazzling colours transformed the entire hall.
items.note: Strong praise for brilliance or spectacular skill.

items.example: The technique was competent but the final composition felt pedestrian.
items.note: A negative critical adjective meaning ordinary and uninspired; not the walking-person sense.

items.pt: evocativo; que desperta imagens ou lembranças
items.example: The photograph is evocative of summer evenings by the sea.
items.note: Frequently evocative of something; brings memories, feelings or images to mind.

items.example: The exhibition's monotonous arrangement was uninspiring.
items.note: Fails to generate interest, enthusiasm or imagination.

items.example: The sculpture raises thought-provoking questions about surveillance.
items.note: Describes a work that stimulates serious reflection.

items.example: The display was visually polished but intellectually unstimulating.
items.note: Opposite of thought-provoking; gives little to think about.

items.example: The miniature contains exquisite details barely visible to the naked eye.
items.note: Particularly fine or delicate beauty and workmanship.

items.example: The colours were striking but the brushwork looked clumsy.
items.note: Lacking delicacy or skill; here contrasts with exquisite.

items.example: The installation offers an intriguing perspective on everyday objects.
items.note: Provokes curiosity because it is unusual or mysterious.

items.example: The endless grey landscapes struck the critic as dreary.
items.note: Suggests dullness and a depressing lack of interest.

items.example: Her control of colour is almost peerless among her contemporaries.
items.note: Highly complimentary adjective meaning unmatched in quality; literary or formal.

items.example: The exhibition included several run-of-the-mill landscapes.
items.note: An informal, generally negative description of something ordinary.

items.pt: irônico; de brincadeira; sem intenção de ser levado ao pé da letra
items.example: The portrait is a tongue-in-cheek tribute to celebrity culture.
items.note: Apparently serious but intended humorously or ironically.

items.example: The video is an earnest appeal for environmental protection.
items.note: Sincere and serious; not necessarily negative, unlike the ironic stance of tongue-in-cheek.

items.example: The museum restored a priceless medieval manuscript.
items.note: So valuable that an ordinary price cannot capture its worth; can also mean extremely funny informally.

items.example: The supposed original turned out to be a worthless copy.
items.note: Having little or no value; context can be financial or artistic.

items.example: The mural shows skilful control of perspective.
items.note: British spelling; US spelling is skillful.

items.example: The restoration was poorly done and damaged the surface.
items.note: Describes weak execution rather than an inherently uninteresting idea.

items.word: paint someone in a particular light
items.example: The biography paints its subject in a surprisingly sympathetic light.
items.note: Figurative pattern: paint somebody in a positive, negative or other light.

items.example: Several shadowy figures appear in the novel without clear motives.
items.note: Metaphor for characters lacking clear definition or reliable detail.

items.example: The witness gave a sketchy account of what had happened.
items.note: From sketch; figuratively means incomplete or insufficiently developed.

items.example: The novel depicts a society struggling with rapid change.
items.note: Formal verb used for representing scenes, people or situations in words or images.

items.example: Her depiction of poverty avoids sentimentality.
items.note: The noun derived from depict; often depiction of something.

items.example: The historian portrays the leader as deeply conflicted.
items.note: Common for representations of a person or character.

items.example: The actor's portrayal of the villain is unusually subtle.
items.note: Noun for the way a character or subject is presented.

items.example: The memoir introduces a colourful cast of eccentric relatives.
items.note: Figuratively describes vivid or interesting people, not only bright hues; British spelling.

items.example: The lead character remained disappointingly colourless.
items.note: In descriptions of people or writing, lacking vitality or distinctiveness.

items.example: Her early experiences shaped her political outlook.
items.note: Metaphorical verb describing how circumstances form someone's development.

items.example: Decades of exile moulded his understanding of belonging.
items.note: British spelling of mold; often moulded by experiences.

items.example: The poet illustrates the theme through recurring images of winter.
items.note: Not confined to making drawings; can explain or demonstrate a point.

items.example: The case offers a useful illustration of the principle.
items.note: Noun for an image or an explanatory example.

items.example: These passages are illustrative of the author's wider argument.
items.note: Formal adjective, typically illustrative of.

items.pt: motivo recorrente; tema ou imagem recorrente
items.example: The recurring mirror motif links the novel's three sections.
items.note: A repeated element or image carrying thematic meaning.

items.example: The essay rejects a black-and-white view of the conflict.
items.note: Figuratively suggests an oversimplified division into opposing categories.

items.example: Her diary entries illuminate the political tensions of the period.
items.note: Formal figurative verb meaning make a complex topic clearer.

items.example: The archival letters offer fresh illumination of the poet's life.
items.note: Noun derived from illuminate; physical light or intellectual clarification.

items.example: The curator gave an illuminating account of the painting's symbolism.
items.note: Describes information or discussion that makes something easier to understand.

items.example: The first sketch already reveals the artist's interest in movement.
items.note: Noun or verb for a quick preliminary representation.

items.example: The painting was created several years before her best-known work.
items.note: Noun related to paint; a work of visual art or the activity itself.

items.example: The book presents a vivid portrait of urban life.
items.note: Can be an artistic depiction or a figurative account.

items.example: The sculptor admired the statue's shapely contours.
items.note: Adjective in the shape family, most often describing an attractive form.

units.title: Unit 22 — Talking about books
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 50–51 (PDF pages 52–53).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Culture and arts · reading, books and literary criticism
learningObjectives: Interpret advanced evaluative language in book blurbs and reviews, including emotional tone and critical praise.
Distinguish journals, memoirs, anthologies, encyclopedias, manuals and logbooks.
Describe absorbing or demanding reading and distinguish formal and informal expressions.
Use precise expressions for historical context, literary protagonists, readership and literary style.

sectionsChecked: A, B and C teaching sections, including numbered definitions and contrasts
Illustrations, margin notes and Common mistakes boxes where present
All facing exercises and relevant answer-key entries

items.pt: texto de apresentação ou sinopse promocional na capa
items.example: The publisher asked the author for a concise blurb.
items.note: Brief promotional text describing a book, often on its back cover.

items.example: The memoir ends with a poignant account of their final meeting.
items.note: Strongly moving, often with sadness or regret.

items.example: The novel is a chronicle of a family over three generations.
items.note: A factual or fictional account of events in chronological sequence.

items.example: The acclaimed novelist returns with an ambitious historical work.
items.note: Publicly praised or admired; commonly an acclaimed author or work.

items.example: The historian presents compelling evidence through personal letters.
items.note: Holds attention or convinces powerfully; may describe stories or arguments.

items.example: The short stories share a deliberately lugubrious atmosphere.
items.note: Unusually mournful or gloomy, sometimes with a disapproving tone.

items.example: The atmosphere is reminiscent of nineteenth-century Gothic fiction.
items.note: Fixed pattern reminiscent of something; suggests a similarity that evokes a memory.

items.example: The novel combines macabre imagery with gentle humour.
items.note: Connected with death, horror or disturbingly gruesome matters.

items.example: The investigation reveals chilling details of the disappearance.
items.note: Frightening in an emotionally unsettling way, often chilling account.

items.pt: livro que prende a atenção; leitura eletrizante
items.example: The courtroom thriller is a genuine page-turner.
items.note: Informal noun for a book that makes you eager to keep reading.

items.example: The biography provides rare insight into the scientist's private life.
items.note: Clear, often sudden understanding; insight into something.

items.example: The archive gives researchers unparalleled access to early drafts.
items.note: Greater or more exceptional than comparable examples.

items.pt: empolgante; eletrizante; que prende a atenção
items.example: The detective novel is gripping from the opening chapter.
items.note: Extremely engaging or suspenseful; a gripping tale or narrative.

items.example: The novel's enigmatic narrator never reveals his motives.
items.note: Difficult to interpret because mysterious or puzzling.

items.example: The plot unfolds through a series of conflicting testimonies.
items.note: A story or event unfolds as it gradually develops or becomes known.

items.example: The author's breathtaking ambition is evident throughout the trilogy.
items.note: Strong praise for something astonishing or magnificent.

items.example: The novel follows a young musician's journey of self-discovery.
items.note: A common literary theme of learning about one's identity or desires.

items.example: The storyteller enchants readers with her playful descriptions.
items.note: To charm or delight greatly; often more literary than please.

items.pt: humor irônico; humor ácido e sutil
items.example: The narrative's wry humour softens its darker moments.
items.note: Humour that is dry, ironic or sceptical, frequently in difficult circumstances.

items.pt: cenas evocativas; passagens que despertam imagens e lembranças
items.example: Her evocative scenes of childhood lend warmth to the narrative.
items.note: Evocative means recalling sensations or memories; useful in literary criticism.

items.pt: epônimo; que dá nome à obra
items.example: The eponymous heroine of the novel is an ambitious journalist.
items.note: A character or person whose name is used as the title of the work.

items.example: The protagonist gradually becomes less reliable as a narrator.
items.note: Central character of a story, distinct from the person who wrote it.

items.example: The novel's engaging voice makes even ordinary events appealing.
items.note: Pleasantly interesting and able to hold attention, often less intense than gripping.

items.example: She kept a journal during her first year abroad.
items.note: Personal record of daily events, observations or learning; different from an academic journal.

items.example: The findings appeared in a peer-reviewed academic journal.
items.note: A regularly published collection of scholarly articles; a journal is not normally called a magazine in this context.

items.example: His memoirs describe his years in diplomatic service.
items.note: An account of aspects of someone's own life; plural is common, singular memoir also exists.

items.example: The actress published a memoir about her early career.
items.note: Singular book-length personal recollection; contrast a memoir with a full biography.

items.example: She consulted an encyclopedia for background information.
items.note: Reference work with explanatory articles, usually organised alphabetically; encyclopaedia is also British spelling.

items.example: The anthology brings together poems by writers from several countries.
items.note: Collection of texts, often by multiple writers and selected around a theme.

items.example: The equipment manual explains how to calibrate the sensor.
items.note: Instruction book describing operation, maintenance or procedures.

items.pt: livro de registros; diário de bordo
items.example: The pilot recorded each flight in a logbook.
items.note: A systematic record of journeys, inspections or events; normally more structured than a personal journal.

items.pt: leitura viciante; leitura da qual é difícil se afastar
items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The account of the expedition makes compulsive reading.
items.note: More formal expression for a book so interesting that one keeps reading.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: I started the novel at midnight and couldn't put it down.
items.note: Informal idiom meaning a book is very absorbing; it refers to the book.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The guide is concise yet surprisingly informative.
items.note: Gives useful factual information, rather than merely entertaining.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: Her speculative novel was ahead of its time in its view of technology.
items.note: Had ideas or methods unusually advanced for the period of creation.

items.pt: produto de sua época; reflexo dos valores de seu tempo
items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The biography is a product of its time and reflects outdated assumptions.
items.note: Explains features of a work as shaped by historical attitudes or circumstances.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The once-scandalous satire now seems relatively tame.
items.note: Lacking force or shock compared with expectations; figurative sense.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The plot relies on old-fashioned attitudes to social class.
items.note: Outdated in style, ideas or customs; not always derogatory.

items.pt: tendencioso em relação a gênero; marcado por viés de gênero
items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The researcher criticised the textbook's gender-biased assumptions.
items.note: Reflecting unfair prejudice or unequal treatment based on gender.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The novel is pleasant but ultimately lightweight.
items.note: In book criticism, not intellectually deep; often mildly negative.

items.pt: leitura leve para antes de dormir
items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The collection of short essays makes ideal bedtime reading.
items.note: Pleasant reading suited to relaxed moments before sleep.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The philosophical chapters are heavy going without prior knowledge.
items.note: An informal expression for material requiring sustained effort; not necessarily bad.

items.pt: envolver-se com um livro; conseguir entrar na história
items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: It took several chapters before I could get into the novel.
items.note: Informal pattern get into something: become interested or absorbed.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The translation introduced the novelist to a much wider readership.
items.note: Collective noun for readers of a particular work or publication.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The essays reached a wide readership beyond universities.
items.note: Natural collocation emphasising a large and varied audience.

items.pt: momentos de percepção profunda; passagens reveladoras
items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The memoir offers moments of insight into the cost of migration.
items.note: A critical phrase for passages that reveal an important understanding.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: This is an engaging tale of friendship across generations.
items.note: A moderately positive evaluation combining engaging with tale.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The journalist provides a chilling account of institutional neglect.
items.note: An unsettling, frightening narrative; chilling is evaluative rather than literal temperature.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The play is a poignant portrayal of an ageing musician.
items.note: A natural critical collocation linking strong feeling with representation.

items.section: C · Describing books and the reading experience
items.example: The trilogy is a breathtaking achievement in historical fiction.
items.note: A strongly positive evaluative collocation in reviews.
